tagline: A desert peninsula built on gas
overview:
Qatar is a small peninsula jutting north into the Persian Gulf from the Arabian mainland, with a single land border, shared with Saudi Arabia. At about 11,600 km² it is roughly the size of Jamaica, and almost all of it is flat desert and salt flat, with no permanent rivers.

Around 3 million people live in Qatar, but only a small fraction are Qatari citizens; most are workers from India, Nepal, Bangladesh, the Philippines and elsewhere. Arabic is the official language and English is used everywhere in business. Doha, the capital, has grown in a generation from a pearling town into a skyline of curved towers, museums and stadiums on the Gulf shore.

Qatar is a monarchy ruled by an emir. It sits above one of the largest natural gas fields on Earth, which has made it one of the richest countries per person, and it hosted the 2022 soccer World Cup, the first in the Arab world.
landAndNature: Qatar is low and dry, the highest ground barely 100 meters above sea level. Summers are ferociously hot, often above 45°C, with humid Gulf air, and rain falls only a few days a year. In the southeast, dunes of the Khor Al Adaid roll right down to a sea inlet, the rare place where large desert dunes meet the sea. Inland lie gravel plains and sabkha, crusted salt flats that shimmer in the heat. Despite the harshness, Arabian oryx, the national animal saved from extinction by captive breeding, roam reserves, and ghaf and acacia trees survive on deep roots. Gulf waters hold dugongs, whale sharks that gather in summer, and the oyster beds that once made the country famous for pearls.
peopleAndCulture: Qatari traditions come from the desert and the sea: falconry, camel racing, dhow sailing and pearl diving. Camel races are now run with lightweight robot jockeys controlled from cars alongside the track. Majlis gatherings, where men sit and talk over cardamom coffee and dates, remain a social anchor. Machboos, spiced rice with meat and dried lime, is the everyday feast dish. Modern Qatar is a place of striking architecture: the Museum of Islamic Art rises from its own island, and the National Museum is shaped like interlocking desert rose crystals. Soccer is the top sport; Qatar won the Asian Cup in 2019 and 2023 and built air-conditioned stadiums for the World Cup, a tournament for which its treatment of migrant construction workers drew international criticism.
history: People have lived along this coast for thousands of years, fishing and trading. Qatar became known for pearl diving, dangerous work in which divers went down on a rope with a nose clip and a basket, and by the 1800s pearls were the backbone of its economy. The Al Thani family emerged as rulers in the 1800s. Qatar came under Ottoman, then British protection, signing a treaty in 1916. The invention of cultured pearls in Japan in the 1920s wrecked the pearl trade and brought hard times. Oil was found in 1939 and exports began after World War II. Qatar became fully independent on September 3, 1971. Gas production from the offshore North Field, starting in the 1990s, transformed the country, and in 1996 it launched the Al Jazeera news network.
funFacts: Qatar has no rivers or lakes, so nearly all its drinking water comes from desalination plants that remove salt from seawater.
Camel races in Qatar use small robot jockeys that owners operate by remote control from cars racing alongside.
The 2022 World Cup was moved to November and December because Qatari summers are too hot for outdoor sport.
Before oil, Qatar's wealth came from pearls gathered by divers who held their breath for two minutes at a time.
Qatar's Khor Al Adaid is called the Inland Sea, a place where large sand dunes run straight down into salt water.
